blogs.title: When Experts Contradict Themselves: The insufficiency of self-contradictory testimony under Johns Hopkins v. Datascope
blogs.description: This post examines the Federal Circuit's application of the Johns Hopkins v. Datascope doctrine to Dr. Wells' shifting testimony on the '134 patent. Dr. Wells initially mapped the claimed 'interference generating signals' to the modeled PIM path, but when confronted on cross-examination with the fact that the modeled PIM path is generated after sampling occurs—making it impossible for the receiver to sample those signals—he pivoted to references to x1 and x2 without ever clearly mapping those signals to the claimed limitations. The post analyzes the tension between the substantial evidence standard and the principle that a party bearing the burden of proof cannot rely on self-contradictory expert testimony, and discusses the implications for patent plaintiffs whose experts change course under cross-examination.

blogs.title: Narrowing Claims Without Surrendering Scope: 'Three Signals,' Prosecution History Disclaimer, and the Clear and Unambiguous Standard
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's prosecution history disclaimer analysis for the '775 patent. Finesse amended its claims during prosecution from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' to overcome a prior art rejection, and AT&T argued this amendment surrendered claim scope over products using only two unique input signals. The court rejected this argument, finding no 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal under Continental Circuits v. Intel, because the examiner's rejection was overcome in part on independent grounds (the prior art addressed active IMPs, not passive IMPs), and because the amendment required three 'separately identifiable' signals but did not require three 'unique' signals. The post explores the doctrinal boundary between narrowing amendments made to overcome prior art and the surrender of claim scope, and discusses how the distinction between 'separately identifiable' and 'unique' signals preserves claim coverage for products using copies of signals.

blogs.title: The Mapping Problem: When Expert Testimony Falls Short of Proving Every Claim Limitation
blogs.description: This post focuses on the Federal Circuit's reversal of noninfringement for the '775 patent based on the evidentiary gap between Dr. Wells' testimony and the claim limitations. The claims required seven specific multiplications of three signals, but Dr. Wells only identified three distinct multiplications in the Nokia documentation and never explained how those three mapped onto the seven claimed multiplications. The post examines the court's insistence that the party bearing the burden of proof must present evidence at trial—not on appeal—linking the accused product to each claim limitation, and analyzes the court's rejection of Finesse's attempt to supplement the record with new mapping arguments raised for the first time in its appellate brief and at oral argument, including its shifting theory that the accused radios perform ten multiplications rather than three.

blogs.title: Judicial Inference vs. Expert Proof: The District Court's Error in Constructing an Infringement Theory from Fragmented Testimony
blogs.description: This post examines the district court's denial of JMOL and its attempt to salvage the jury's infringement verdict by inferring an infringement theory that Finesse's own expert never clearly articulated. The district court found that 'Dr. Wells is clearly referring to x1 and x2' despite Dr. Wells never testifying to that mapping, and pieced together fragments of testimony from pages ninety pages apart in the trial record. The Federal Circuit rejected this approach, emphasizing that courts cannot construct infringement theories from disjointed expert testimony when the expert himself never offered a coherent explanation. The post discusses the proper role of the trial judge in evaluating JMOL motions, the limits of permissible inference from trial evidence, and the Fifth Circuit's 'so strongly and overwhelmingly' standard for JMOL reversals, which the Federal Circuit applied here to correct the district court's overly deferential posture toward the jury verdict.
